posts.title: The Reasoning Behind the Second Amendment
posts.summary:
A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of
the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.
-Second Amendment
posts.imageAlt: The Signing of the Declaration of Independance
posts.body:
The second amendment is a very controversial and misunderstood part of the constitution.
The second amendment is not about hunting, it is about self defense. It was written to allow
citizens to defend themselves against other people and institutions, such as the government.
It is essential that we understand exactly what it means so we can continue to have a free
state.

You might wonder why an individual needs to own a gun in the first place. Many critics of
the second amendment say that it doesn't pertain to individuals, that the clause "well
regulated," means government regulated, and "Militia" means government military.
However, if you look into the writings of the authors of the Bill of Rights, their reasoning
becomes clearer. For starters, the American Revolution was fresh in the minds of the
founding fathers. They understood what tyranny looked like. They understood the
importance of an armed populace. We would not have won the Revolutionary War if our
populace was not already armed. The arguments against the individuality of the second
amendment do not hold up against the writings of the time. George Mason said: "Who are
the militia? They consist now of the whole people, except a few public officers." Richard
Henry Lee said:"Militias, when properly formed, are in fact the people themselves and
include all men capable of bearing arms. [...] To preserve liberty it is essential that the
whole body of the people always possess arms and be taught alike, especially when young,
how to use them." and, "To preserve liberty, it is essential that the whole body of people
always possess arms." There are dozens of similar quotes by the founding fathers that
clearly show that they intended for individual citizens to have the right to own guns.

If it was true that the right to bear arms only pertains to groups of people, then the other
rights listed in the Bill of Rights, like freedom of religion, assembly, and speech, would also
not be individual rights. If they are not individual rights, then we should stop calling them
rights. We should instead call them privileges, because when one part of a group abuses
their privileges, then the remaining members of the group also lose their privileges. In this
scenario, the elite or ruling members get to decide when to take away privileges. Therefore,
it is logical to portray the second amendment as a privilege, and then remove that privilege
to increase your power. The main reason many of our leaders want to take away our second-
amendment right is to remove resistance to tyranny. They do not truly care about
preservation of life or they would be just as concerned about changing other policies that
result in the shedding of innocent blood, such as abortion. They only want to have unlimited
and unchecked power.

An armed populace is one of the ways ordinary citizens can help retain their rights.
However, the best way to keep freedom, is to fight the ideological battles. False ideas that
are contrary to God's Word are the problem. The church needs to stand up and boldly teach
the truth.

posts.title: Stonewall Jackson: The Man Behind the Legend
posts.summary:
To understand what made Stonewall Jackson great you must understand his beliefs.
His battlefield excellence flowed from his core doctrines.
posts.imageAlt: Portrait of Confederate General Thomas Stonewall Jackson
posts.body:
Few historical military figures are as fascinating as Confederate General Thomas “Stonewall” Jackson. His renowned tactical brilliance throughout the American Civil War earned him respect from allies and enemies alike. Yet to truly understand what made Jackson such a great leader, one must look beyond his battlefield maneuvers. His battlefield genius was not just the result of his own intellect, but it was deeply rooted in a set of unwavering personal beliefs and doctrines. Jackson’s faith in the God of the Bible, sense of duty, and discipline shaped who he was both on and off the battlefield. By exploring these core beliefs we can better understand what made him such an effective military commander.
 
Thomas Jonathan Jackson was born in Clarksburg, Virginia on January 21, 1824. However, it is not certain that this was his actual birth date because his family had no documented record of the event, and he could not remember with certainty the exact date. Clarksburg is now in the state of West Virginia, but Jackson died before West Virginia became a state. So he will forever be remembered as a Virginian.

Jackson’s father died when he was three, leaving his widowed mother with three fatherless children. His father had been a Freemason, and the local Masonic Lodge gave them a small one-room house to live in. His mother lived there the rest of her life, teaching the children and supporting herself financially by taking in sewing. In 1830, when Jackson was six years old, she married again. At this time, she sent Jackson and his brother to live with their uncle Robinson because she thought they could be better provided for with their uncle.

His mother only lived for about a year after her second marriage. She had very delicate health and was significantly weakened by the birth of her last son, named Wirt. She sent for her two sons to give them her farewell blessings, and after lingering a few weeks, passed away. Her husband said that, “Death for her had no sting; the grave could claim no victory.” (Jackson 17)

Being only seven at the time, his mother’s death undoubtedly left a strong impression on Jackson. Despite only knowing her for a short time, she instilled a good character in her sons that would serve them well throughout their life. After his mother’s death he wrote to his aunt Mrs. Neale:

“Though I have reached home, yet the pleasures enjoyed under your hospitable roof, and in your family circle, have not been dissipated. . . . I stopped to see the Hawk's Nest, and the gentleman with whom I put up was at my mother's burial, and accompanied me to the cemetery for the purpose of pointing out her grave to me but I am not certain that he found it. There was no stone to mark the spot. Another gentleman, who had the kindness to go with us, stated that a wooden head or foot board with her name on it had been put up, but it was no longer there. A depression in the earth only marked her resting-place. When standing by her grave, I experienced feelings to which I was until then a stranger. I was seeking the spot partly for the purpose of erecting something to her precious memory. On Saturday last I lost my porte-monnaie, and in it was the date of my mother's birth. Please give me the date in your next letter.” ( Jackson 17-18)

After Jackson’s death, a Confederate soldier visited the graveyard and said, “The location is so beautiful, and the view it commands so extensive and exquisite, that it is worthy of being well cared for.” (Jackson 18-19) Captain Thomas D. Ransom had a marble slab placed on her grave after the Civil War, with an inscription giving the dates of her death and birth, and the words “A tribute to the mother of Stonewall Jackson, by one of his old brigade.” (Jackson 18-19)
After his mother’s death, Jackson was sent back to live with his father’s relatives on the old Jackson homestead in Lewis County, Virginia. He and his sister Laura lived with his step-grandmother Jackson until her death, and afterwards lived with his uncle Cummins. His uncle was a kind man who provided everything necessary for Jackson and his siblings.

By Lewis County standards, the Jackson family was rich. They owned land up and down the West Fork River Valley, a large saw mill, a grain mill, a general store, carpenter shops, blacksmith shops, and their house was the finest in the area. The Jacksons also owned a large number of sheep, cows, chickens, and orchards. The estate was managed by Jackson’s Uncle Cummins, who was a very good business man with a good reputation in the area.

As a child, Jackson and his siblings, when not in school, occupied themselves with making maple sugar from the family's maple trees, trapping, or hunting rabbits. Jackson tried to learn to play the violin, but not having the gift of music, he was never very good. Jackson proved to be a capable and diligent worker at the Jackson family mill, which was the largest saw mill in the area. He proved to be so capable that he was set to oversee all of the laborers in getting the largest trees out of the forest, conveying them to the mill, and sawing them into lumber. He showed great diligence, efficiency, and endurance in the tasks he was given. One who knew him well at the time said:

“He was a youth of exemplary habits, of indomitable will and undoubted courage. He possessed in an eminent degree a talent for mathematics, and was unwilling, while at school, to acknowledge his incapacity ‘give him time’ to solve any proposition. He was not what is nowadays termed brilliant, but he was one of those untiring, matter-of-fact persons who would never give up when he engaged in an undertaking until he accomplished his object. He learned slowly, but when he got learning into his head, he never forgot it. He was not quick to decide, except when excited, and then when he made up his mind to do a thing, he did it on short notice and in quick time. Thus, while on his way to school, an overgrown rustic behaved rudely to one of the school-girls. Jackson was fired at his cowardly conduct, and told him he must apologize at once, or he would ‘thrash him’. The big fellow, supposing that he was an overmatch for him, refused, whereupon Jackson pitched into him, and gave him a severe pounding.” (Jackson 27)

While working at the mill, Jackson developed a growing desire for knowledge. He had not received much formal schooling in his childhood, and he desired to educate himself and gain a higher position to keep up the prestige of his name. An opportunity for higher education came when a young man from his congressional district, upon being appointed to West Point, decided that the strict discipline was not for him. This left a vacancy that Jackson could fill. His Uncle Cummins suggested the idea to him, and he enthusiastically accepted it.

Jackson then began to use all of his effort to try to secure the position. Friends and neighbors wrote to their senator asking to him give Jackson the nomination. The senator agreed and asked Jackson to come to Washington to be approved by the Secretary of Defense. The Secretary, upon seeing his good character, approved him and said,''Sir, you have a good name. Go to West Point, and the first man who insults you knock him down, and have it charged to my account!" (Jackson 32)

Jackson was not very good at many of the subjects assigned to him. Due to his rural upbringing and lack of previous education, he had difficulty understanding what was being taught, and often spent hours studying. He would never let an assignment go past its due date, but worked hard on it until it was finished. He did well enough to pass most of what was required, and the subjects he did not pass he was allowed to advance in by working extra in other areas. 

One of the most interesting things about him at this time was his physical ailments. Some who knew him would describe him as a hypochondriac; however he had a real chronic condition, uveitis, which made it difficult to use his eyes. He felt pain just trying to focus his eyes on a subject, and he was extremely sensitive to light. This sensitivity led to one of his stranger habits: sitting alone in the dark with his eyes closed, mentally preparing for the next day. He was in such pain that, at times, he submerged his head in cold water with his eyes open multiple times a day. To those who did not understand his suffering, these practices would have undoubtedly seemed odd. His eye problems occurred intermittently throughout his adult life. However, his dyspepsia seems to have been a more constant problem. In the 1800’s, dyspepsia was a catch-all term for most digestive problems. It is not clear exactly what Jackson had, but it caused him discomfort which was sometimes severe. He sought a lot of water cures for his dyspepsia. He spent weeks at a time at mineral springs all across the eastern United States. He visited such establishments about fourteen times in his life, and claimed that they gave him some relief from his symptoms. He also had a strict diet. He sometimes adhered to a diet of stale bread and cold water, eating meat less than once a month. He spent one summer eating nothing but fresh buttermilk and cornbread. As with everything else, he did not change his personal habits when in public, and frequently brought his own food to dinner parties.

He was obsessive over his health. He worried about his throat, kidneys, heart, stomach, and everything else. He followed the latest health trends, like inhaling glycerin and silver, and swallowing ammonia. He was a very avid walker, walking at least five miles a day. He was also involved in some sort of strange looking jumping exercises.

Jackson’s health beliefs were not the results of naivety; they were a result of his earnestness, profound sense of purpose, and his unashamed persistence in that purpose. He never let his behavior be sullen, gloomy, or mean spirited. He was stern, but polite to those around him, and was pleasant to be around.

Jackson gained his first combat experience in the Mexican-American War. On June 30, 1846, he received the rank of second lieutenant of artillery. While he fought well at Vera Cruz and Contreras, his best battle performance was at the Battle of Chapultepec. Chapultepec was a large castle on a rock outlook that was the US Army’s last objective before reaching Mexico City. Jackson’s army unit, which consisted of two six-pound cannons and an infantry regiment, found themselves in a causeway beneath the castle’s battlements. They were receiving fire from thousands of muskets stationed inside the castle. They would be further exposed if they advanced or retreated, so they readied the two guns and began firing back.

Jackson’s cannons faced eight Mexican cannons at very short range. All twelve of Jackson’s horses were killed or severely wounded, and one of the cannons was hit and became unmovable. The infantry, seeing the shells bursting around them, fled into the bushes on the side of the causeway. Jackson remained on the causeway, pacing back and forth alone, while shells exploded all around him. A cannon-ball even bounced right between his legs. He yelled at his men,“There is no danger! See? I am not hit!” (Jackson 43) At first he had no takers, but one sergeant returned to the causeway and commenced firing the cannon.

When General William J. Worth, Jackson’s commanding officer, rode up he was amazed to see Jackson, who had been abandoned by his troops save one sergeant, fighting a duel with the Mexican cannons in front of the main US lines. Jackson was ordered to retire but refused, saying that it was more dangerous to retreat than to advance. Reinforcements soon arrived and Jackson got the second gun working. They began to fire more furiously on the Mexicans than before. General Worth sent a brigade up the hill Jackson was firing on, and the defenses crumbled. Chapultepec soon fell. Jackson, who was still eager to fight, joined General Scott’s attack on Santa Anna’s remaining troops. He quickly found wagons to haul his two cannons and set out at a fast pace for San Cosme Gate. He was moving so fast that he was well out in front of the rest of the army. He located some cavalry down the road and fired on them, which ripped large holes in their column. The next morning he began shelling San Cosme Gate and the city soon was overthrown.

Jackson’s exploits became big news in the army. He was mentioned in the General’s official report, which was rare at the time. General Worth, though commanding a different division of troops, gives the following tribute:

“After advancing some four hundred yards, we came to a battery which had been assailed by a portion of Magruder's field-guns, particularly the section under the gallant Jackson, who, although he had lost most of his horses and many of his men, continued chivalrously at his post, combating with noble courage.” (Jackson 42-43)

He was invited to General Scott’s reception for army officers, and received high praise from his commanding generals. He had only been in active duty for fifteen months, and he was promoted to first lieutenant and then major, which was the fastest anyone in the army at the time had been promoted.

After the Mexican American war was over, Jackson was stationed at Fort Hamilton in Florida, and then at Fort Meade in Maryland. He remained at Fort Meade for two years, and then was elected as Professor of Natural and Experimental Philosophy and Artillery Tactics in the Military Academy of Virginia (VMI). He was given an annual salary of twelve-hundred dollars with an additional stipend to pay for housing. Jackson’s friend Reverend Dabney wrote of the selection:

“The prosperity and growth of the Military Institute calling for another instructor in this department, the eyes of its governors were directed to Major Jackson, by his high character, scholarship, and brilliant career in Mexico. Other names were submitted by the Faculty of West Point,among which may be mentioned those of General George B. M'Clellan, General Reno, and General Rosecranz of the present Federal armies, and the distinguished General G. W. Smith of the Confederate army. But the high testimonials given to Major Jackson, and his birth as a Virginian, secured the preference of the visitors, who elected him by a unanimous vote.” (Dabney 61)
 
His career as a professor was respected, but not popular. No one doubted his intellectual skill, but he was not very good at helping those who were lagging behind in class catch up with the other students. The better students understood and followed along relatively well, but the students lagging behind fell further and further behind.

After moving to Lexington, Jackson met one of the town’s distinct persons: the Reverend Dr. George Junkin. Junkin was the president of George Washington College, which was founded in 1749 by George Washington himself. While performing his academic duties, Junkin conducted regular services at the George Washington College Chapel. Being an intellectual and deeply religious man, Junkin was the kind of older man that was missing in Jackson’s life. Jackson was a frequent visitor of the Junkin’s parlor. They spent many hours discussing theology and Presbyterian doctrine. Junkin was fond of Jackson, and enjoyed his company. Junkin’s biographer described their relations as,“those of a fond father and an affectionate son.” (Gwynne 142) However, there was another reason that Jackson was interested in the Junkin family. He was courting one of the Reverend's eight children, Ellie. She was a year younger than Jackson, and a devout Presbyterian. They got along well, and sometime in early 1853 were engaged. The two were married on August 4, 1853 in a modest ceremony in the Junkin’s parlor at Washington College.

The Jacksons had a happy marriage, and were expecting their first child by 1854. Ellie expected to have no issues considering her mother had given birth successfully nine times. On Sunday, October 22, 1854, Ellie went into labor. A local doctor was in attendance, as well as some family members. It is not entirely clear what went wrong, but Ellie delivered a stillborn son – a tragedy for the Jacksons. Jackson wrote about the following events:

“The doctor said that all is well. The womb closed apparently healthily, though the child was dead. The doctor left the house for a few minutes, and I was admitted into the room and upon observing her in agonizing pain I desired the doctor to return. He soon after entered, but a sudden change had taken place: the womb had relaxed and in a short time her spirit took its flight.” (Gwyne 147)

Some doctors believe that Ellie had an excruciatingly painful hemorrhage that the doctor could not stop, and she bled to death.

Jackson was shattered. In a letter to his sister he said,“The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away, blessed be the name of the Lord,” and,“ I can willingly submit to anything if God strengthens me.” (Gwyne 148) He was at peace only through faith in God and His promises to do what is best for His people. At that time, he wanted more than anything to join Ellie in heaven.

Jackson took a three month tour of Europe in the summer of 1856, and used the time to overcome his sadness over the death of his wife. After he returned to the States, he went to Charlotte, North Carolina to call on Miss Mary Anna Morison. They had met while she was in Lexington visiting her sister. At twenty-seven years of age, she was intelligent, pious, and very refined. She was the daughter of Dr. Robert Hall Morison, who had founded Davidson College in 1837. The courtship lasted only a day. Jackson returned to Lexington an engaged man. They were married on July 16, 1857, in Anna’s home in North Carolina. They bought a house in Lexington, which immediately became the center of their lives. Just off of Main Street, it was a block away from the Presbyterian church and a ten minute walk from VMI.

Jackson’s best qualities were his devoutly Christian beliefs. He was a deacon at the Presbyterian church in Lexington, and despite his weakness in public speaking, led prayer services there from time to time. He was well known for his Christian attitude and love of the commands of God. As one of his friends put it, “God was in all his thoughts… God, God Himself, the living, personal, and present God… possessed his whole being.”(Gwyne 146) Jackson himself summed it up best in a statement he made in response to a friend asking him about the command to “pray without ceasing.”
“ I can give you," he said, '' my idea of it by illustration, if you will allow it, and will not think that I am setting myself up as a model for others. I have so fixed the habit in my own mind that I never raise a glass of water to my lips without lifting my heart to God in thanks and prayer for the water of life. Then, when we take our meals, there is the grace. Whenever I drop a letter in the post-office, I send a petition along with it for God's blessing upon its mission and the person to whom it is sent. When I break the seal of a letter just received, I stop to ask God to prepare me for its contents, and make it a messenger of good. When I go to my class-room and await the arrangement of the cadets in their places, that is my time to intercede with God for them. And so in every act of the day I have made the practice habitual.” (Jackson 72-73)

When the friend asked if he ever forgot to do this he said: “I can hardly say that I do; the habit has become almost as fixed as to breathe.” (Jackson 73) He was frequently seen praying for God to be with them before and during battles. He believed in Divine Providence and desired to serve God in all that he did.

He kept the Sabbath strictly. He always attended church twice on Sunday and taught two Sabbath schools. He refrained, as much as possible, from worldly conversation, and if secular topics were introduced in his family, he would kindly say with a smile, “We will talk about that to-morrow.”(Jackson 75) He never traveled on Sunday, never took his mail from the post office, nor permitted a letter of his own to travel on that day by always calculating the time required to reach its destination. His wife said of him:“One so strict in his own Sabbath observance naturally believed that it was wrong for the government to carry the mails on Sunday. Any organization which exacted secular labor of its employees on the Lord's day was, in his opinion, a violator of God's law.” (Jackson 75)

In regard to Jackson’s views on slavery during the Civil War, his wife summed it up the best.

“It has been said that General Jackson “fought for slavery and the Southern Confederacy with the unshaken conviction that both were to endure.” This statement is true with regard to the latter, but I am very confident that he would never have fought for the sole object of perpetuating slavery. It was for her constitutional rights that the South resisted the North, and slavery was only comprehended among those rights. He found the institution a responsible and troublesome one, and I have heard him say that he would prefer to see the negroes free, but he believed that the Bible taught that slavery was sanctioned by the Creator himself, who maketh men to differ, and instituted laws for the bond and the free. He therefore accepted slavery, as it existed in the Southern States, not as a thing desirable in itself, but as allowed by Providence for ends which it was not his business to determine. At the same time, the negroes had no truer friend, no greater benefactor. Those who were servants in his own house he treated with the greatest kindness, and never was more happy or more devoted to any work than that of teaching the colored children in his Sunday-school.” (Jackson 142-143)

Jackson owned six slaves, three of which he had personally acquired and three of which were given to him as a wedding present by Anna’s father. Jackson’s first slave, Albert, came to him and asked him to buy him so that he would be allowed to buy his freedom by paying back the purchase price. Jackson, who was a bachelor at the time, had little use for Albert’s services, so he initially rented him out as a waiter to VMI for $120 a year. When Albert came down with a protracted illness, and could not work, Jackson took him in and cared for him. The Civil War started before Albert finished paying Jackson, and Albert went his own way. The second slave Jackson purchased was an older woman named Amy, who was about to be sold to pay a debt. She too begged Jackson to purchase her. He found her a loving Christian home to lie in until he had one of his own. She showed her gratitude by serving him faithfully. His wife Anna described her as, “a real treasure,” and one of the best cooks they ever had. After the Civil War started Amy became sick. Jackson paid for her lodging, medical expenses, and finally her funeral. The third slave Jackson personally acquired was a four-year-old girl named Emma, who had been left an orphan. He hoped that one day she could help Anna with the housekeeping. Despite a seeming learning disability, Jackson tried to teach her the Catechism and about the Bible.

The other three slaves, Hetty, who had been with Anna since her birth, and her two teenage sons, were a gift from Anna’s father. Not much is known about Jackson’s interactions with his slaves. The few remaining accounts describe him as a loving, kind, and stern master who sought what was good for those under his authority.

In 1855, he started a Sunday school for blacks at his Presbyterian church. His wife said,“His interest in that race was simply because they had souls to save.” (Jackson 77-78) Eighty to one-hundred blacks regularly attended. Jackson read from the Bible, prayed, and sang songs with them. At the time, teaching a black to read and write was illegal in the state of Virginia, but Jackson thought that their ability to read the Bible was very important. So he sought to obey God rather than man. Overall, he was well respected and liked by the blacks in Lexington.

As the first states seceded from the Union in 1861, the issue of secession became one of the center issues in Virginia. Jackson was always for the Union, but he was also a firm state’s rights man. He was never a secessionist and maintained that it would be better for the South to fight for her rights as a member the Union rather than leaving it. However, he believed that the individual states had the right to defend themselves. When South Carolina seceded and took possession of Fort Sumter, Lincoln called on the other states to provide seventy-five thousand men to put down the perceived “rebellion.” Virginia hesitated no longer, and seceded on April 17, 1861. Virginia then tried to prepare for the inevitable struggle. Despite the gathering storm, Jackson displayed no undo anxiety. He prayed more frequently that if it were God’s will, war might be averted and the whole land might be at peace. While a guest at Jackson’s house, Rev. Dr. J. B. Ramsey recorded Jackson’s thoughts on the Union’s dissolution:

“Why,” said he,“should Christians be disturbed about the dissolution of the Union? It can come only by God's permission, and will only be permitted if for His people's good for does He not say, ‘All things work together for good to them that love God ?’ I cannot see how we should be distressed about such things, whatever be their consequences.” (Jackson 142 )

The clouds of war were close to bursting. Virginia’s governor “Honest John Letcher,” notified VMI’s superintendent to prepare the advanced classes of cadets to use as drill masters. They had to be ready to go to Richmond at a moment’s notice with General Jackson as their commander. At dawn April 21, 1861, the door-bell rang, and the order came that Jackson was to bring the cadets to Richmond immediately. Without eating breakfast he repaired to VMI and began making preparations to begin the march to Richmond. He set the departure time for one-o-clock, returned home, ate breakfast, and took his Bible and began to read the passage in Corinthians – “For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle be dissolved, we have a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens."(2 Corinthians 5:1) He then prayed that if it was consistent with God’s will, He would avert the threatening danger and grant them peace. Jackson’s pastor, Dr. White, held a short religious service that ended at one-o-clock sharp, as Jackson had requested. They began marching precisely at one-o-clock. He left his home in Lexington with a firm trust in God, and hoped to return again. However, his footstep would never again cross the threshold of his house. After this point, his life was devoted to his beloved southern land.

On May 2, Virginia adopted the Constitution of the Confederate States, appointed Commissioners to their Congress, and aligned their values to those of the Confederacy. When Virginia seceded, it prompted North Carolina, Tennessee, Arkansas, and Missouri, to join the Confederacy. On May 20, the Confederate Congress was adjourned from Columbia to Richmond. The President of the Confederacy, Jefferson Davis, also moved to Richmond.

After marching to Staunton, the VMI cadets were transferred by rail to Richmond. On April 27, 1861, Jackson was ordered to take command of Harper’s Ferry. He implemented order and discipline to the troops stationed there, who were largely militia groups from the Shenandoah Valley.

Jackson was relived of his command of Harpers Ferry by General Joseph E. Johnston in June 1861. The Virginia regiments, which were at different posts, were now broken up and reorganized into the Stonewall Brigade. It was composed of the 2nd,4th, 5th, 27th, and 33rd Virginia Regiments.

The first major engagement of the Stonewall Brigade was the First Battle of Manassas. The Confederate troops were a motley group of individuals. Some wore blue uniforms, while some wore gray uniforms, and others were even in civilian clothes. Most of the Confederate troops had smooth-bore muskets, whereas the Union troops were largely armed with rifled muskets. Jackson’s troops had, for the most part, never fought before.

The junction of Manassas was a hot, flat crossroads thirty miles away from Washington, DC. The Confederate army had decided to defend Manassas at all costs because it was a major railroad junction between Richmond and northern Virginia. The Confederate army fortified the area surrounding the junction by digging trenches and dirt mounds. In the midst of these trenches, a three-ton naval cannon had somehow been dragged into place. This cannon could hurl thirty-two pound balls. The Federal strategy was to flank the Confederate troops on their left, thus positioning the large mass of Federal troops on a weak area of the Confederate line. The Confederate strategy was to flank the Union flank. The Confederate commander was General Joseph E. Johnston. The Union commander was Irvin McDowell.

Jackson and his troops arose at 3:30 am, ate a hasty breakfast, and began their march towards the battlefield. At 9:30 am, Jackson received orders to move towards the Stone Bridge, and then set his troops on a brutally fast march. His men were running down the dusty roads as fast as Jackson could get them to go. Along Jackson’s route he ran into a routed General Bernard Bee. Bee said, “General, they are driving us,” to which Jackson replied, “Sir, we will give them the bayonet.” (Dabney 222) Bee’s retreating forces were the result of General McDowell’s massive flank march. Jackson selected a defensive position on the southeastern edge of the plateau on Henry Hill. There was a wooded area there that would provide the Virginians some cover from artillery fire. He had his troops lie down along the edge of the woods with fourteen canons aligned in front of them.

General Johnston, upon realizing the the battle was not where they thought it was going to be, ordered his troops to Jackson’s position. At 1:00 pm the new battle line was in place, with the Virginians lying in the woods fronted by the artillery pieces. At about 2:30 pm, an artillery duel began between the Union and Confederate cannons. Jackson was riding up and down the Confederate lines on his horse, Little Sorrel, repeating, “Steady men. Steady. All is well.” (Gwynne 88) One soldier of the 33rd Virginia regiment said, as they observed him, they, “Saw the warrior and forgot the eccentric man.” (Gwynne 89) As Jackson was talking to General John D. Imboden he raised his left had towards Imboden, and “as he spoke, he jerked down his hand, and I saw that blood was streaming from it. I exclaimed, ‘General, you are wounded.’ He replied, as he drew a handkerchief from his breast-pocket, and began to bind it up, ‘Only a scratch — a mere scratch,’ and galloped away along his line.” (Imboden 236)

Jackson’s short-range artillery duel with the Federals was getting the better of them. The Federal rifled parrot guns did no better at short range than the smoothbore canons of the 
Confederates. Jackson repelled a small Federal attack on his right and held his position in the pine woods for hours. At this time Bee was trying to locate what was left of his troops and came upon the 4th Alabama, who were resting from their fighting earlier that day. Bee asked them if they would follow him back to the fighting. All one hundred men said a resounding yes, and Bee, pointing to his left toward the pine woods said, “Yonder stands Jackson like a stone wall. Let’s go to his assistance.” (Gwynne 90)

Now the battle changed; it was no longer an artillery duel. The 14th New York regiment attacked the 33rd Virginia, and the men on Jackson’s left began collapsing. The emboldened New Yorkers attacked the Confederate center of the 4th and 27th regiments – who had been lying down in the woods for several hours. Jackson told his men,“Reserve your fire until they come within 50 yards, then fire and give them the bayonet, and when you charge yell like Furies.” (Gwynne 91) Jackson’s men did what they were told to do, and released a volley of shot and canister on the New Yorkers, repelling them. The New Yorkers regrouped, attacked again, and were repelled again. The New Yorkers tried for a third time to break the Confederate center, but were cut to pieces by the Virginians. The Yankee battle line faltered and then completely broke.

Jackson then prepared his men to charge. Jackson’s Virginians swept out of the woods, screaming, and chased the retreating Yankees towards the deadly Federal batteries on the far edge of Henry Hill. The screaming noise the Confederates made was described by the Union troops as inhuman, feral, and unearthly. The noise would become known as the “Rebel Yell”, and would become the stuff of nightmares for Union troops.

Jackson’s two regiments pierced the heart of the Union lines and captured the Federal guns. “The charge of Jackson’s men was terrific,” wrote Private John Casler of the 33rd Virginia regiment(Gwyne 92). General Beauregard ordered more troops to pour into the field. The whole open surface of the plateau was swept clean of Federals.

Jackson’s five brigades were at the white-hot center of the battle for hours, fighting over the possession of the Federal batteries. They sustained the largest casualties of any Confederate regiments during the battle. Union General McDowell’s men made a successful third surge against Jackson’s men, and recaptured the batteries. McDowell wired to DC that the battle was a Union victory, but he was very wrong, because the battle was not done.

Johnston’s army of the Shenandoah arrived bringing fresh Virginian troops to the front. These new troops drove the Union off of the hill and recaptured the hill. McDowell ordered a retreat and the Union commanders tried to rally their men, but to no avail. The Union troops were in a mass panic, and their only thought was to flee to Washington for safety. They reeled by the same Bull Run fords they had crossed earlier, leaving behind provisions, overcoats, knapsacks, blankets, muskets, canteens, and cartridge boxes. Many civilians from Washington DC had come out to watch what they thought was going to be a good whipping for the Rebels. They were now being trampled by a panicked mob of routed soldiers. Some of the onlookers tried to get the soldiers to change their minds. They called them cowards, denounced them in offensive terms, and even threatened to shoot them, but to no avail.

When Jefferson Davis arrived on the battlefield, he was informed by Confederate stragglers far in the rear that the battle was lost. Upon arrival at the front Davis cried “I am President Davis! Follow me back to the field.”(Gwyne 94) Jackson did not hear Davis say this, but when he was told by General McGuire, he stood up, took off his cap, and said, “We have whipped them. They ran like sheep. Give me 10,000 men and I can take Washington tomorrow!” (Gwyne 96) It soon became evident to everyone the magnitude of their victory. Cheers resounded throughout the South. Some even thought that this was the end of the war.

After the Federal rout at Manassas, General McClellan (Little Mac) brought his new Army of the Potomac out for a military parade. Spectators came out to watch the sea of blue uniforms dotted with shining bayonets march around in formation. The Federal Army of the Potomac was around 150,000 strong, opposing the 40,000 Virginians. This was an incredible mismatch considering the Federals were not only more numerous but also better equipped than the rebel army. Little Mac for a long time refused to take his almost quarter-million troops into Virginia. He had different reasons at different times. Sometimes his army was not ready, or sometimes the Rebel troop strength was too much.

Jackson camped his brigade just a few miles from the Manassas battlefield. He was busy doing what newly minted brigadiers were not supposed to do: think in sweeping geopolitical, military, and economic terms. He had come up with a plan to invade and lay waste to the North’s cities, armies, and industries. He laid it all out before Major General G. W. Smith:

“We could cut off the communications of Washington, force the Federal government to abandon the capital, beat McClellan's army if it came out against us in the open country, destroy industrial establishments wherever we found them, break up the lines of interior commercial intercourse, close the coal mines, seize and, if necessary, destroy the manufactories and commerce of Philadelphia, and of other large cities within our reach; take hold the narrow neck of country between Pittsburgh and Lake Erie; subsist mainly on the country we traverse, and making unrelenting war amidst their home, force the people of the north to understand what it will cost them to hold the South in the Union at the bayonet’s point.” (Gwynne 73)

The leading generals in the South did not agree with Jackson. They preferred to take a defensive position defending cities rather than invading the enemy territory. The South chose to wait until McClellan was ready to invade them, which they would later learn was a mistake. Jackson possessed the attributes to exploit the weaknesses of his disorganized and sometimes timid foes. He knew the terrain well and often used it in unconventional ways to his advantage. He also had the uncommon ability to inspire his troops to incredible feats of marching and fighting.

Jackson’s Valley Campaign started out with a tactical loss, but a strategic victory for the Confederacy at Kernstown Virginia on March 23, 1862. He was ordered to march towards Harper’s Ferry, so he began north at a furious pace with about 3,000 men. He received faulty intelligence that led him to believe he was attacking a small detachment, when in fact, he was attacking about 9,000 Federals. He attacked the Federals with such ferocity that President Lincoln thought they were a much larger force. This caused Lincoln to order Major General Nathaniel Banks to stay in the Shenandoah Valley, and Major General Irwin McDowell to stay near Fredericksburg, thus subtracting 50,000 men from McClellan’s invasion force. This move considerably delayed and weakened McClellan in his advance towards Richmond.

Banks chased Jackson’s troops to Mount Jackson, but called off further pursuit due to supply chain issues. Meanwhile, McClellan’s Peninsula Campaign was underway, and General Johnston relocated most of the Confederate Army to defend Richmond. This left Jackson’s men isolated in the Shenandoah Valley. Jackson’s orders were to to prevent Banks from seizing Staunton and the Virginia and Tennessee Railroad.

Once Jackson received Richard S. Ewell’s 8,500-man division, for reinforcements, he marched his troops to a village named McDowell in pursuit of General Robert Huston Milroy. The Federal generals realized they were badly outnumbered, and attacked Sitlington Hill to try to prevent Jackson from placing artillery pieces there. They were repelled from the hill and Jackson attempted to pursue, but the Federals were thirteen miles in the lead. The Federals took up a defensive position overlooking the road to Franklin, West Virginia, and Jackson did not attempt to attack them.

Jackson created a plan to destroy General Banks’ army by sending calvary units north to make Banks think they were going to attack Strasburg. In reality, Jackson planned to attack a small Federal outpost at Front Royal and make Banks’ position untenable. On May 23, 1862, Jackson attacked, and quickly pushed them out out of the town. Jackson sent cavalry companies to chase the fleeing Federals. The Federals tried to reform a line and fight, but they were quickly broken by the Confederate cavalry. The Federals had 773 casualties, while Jackson had only 36 casualties. Jackson’s men captured about $300,000 of Federal supplies, and Banks soon became known as “Commissary Banks” because of the many supplies the Confederates won from him during the Valley Campaign.

Banks withdrew from Strasburg, Virginia and marched towards Winchester, Virginia. Jackson raced to Winchester ahead of Banks, and Jackson’s men harassed Bank’s men all along the Valley Turnpike. The Federals withdrew over the Potomac having suffered large casualty rates.

Banks’ hasty ejection from the Shenandoah Valley at the hand of Jackson worried Washington. They thought he might continue north and threaten the capital. Lincoln ordered an elaborate offensive to trap Jackson and destroy his force. He ordered General Fremont to engage Jackson and Ewell at Harrisonburg, Virginia. Banks was then to recross the Potomac and pursue Jackson if he moved up the Shenandoah Valley. McDowell was to wait at Front Royal and attack and pursue Jackson’s column as it passed by, and crush Jackson’s army against Fremont’s position. However, Lincoln’s plan was complex and required different commands to coordinate with each other. Fremont did not obey his orders the way Lincoln had hoped, which put the Federals in a position where all that could be accomplished was a pincer-like movement on Jackson’s forces. This would have to be precisely timed in order to work.

Jackson marched his men down the Valley Pike and outpaced his pursuers. The two Federal armies converged on the southwestern end of Massanutten Mountain, and Jackson could have escaped by going through Brown’s Gap towards Charlottesville and marching to Richmond. However, he chose to finish his work in the Valley and destroy the two opposing armies.

He recognized the importance of the small town of Port Republic. If he could destroy the bridges in this area, he could keep the two Federal armies from joining forces against him. On June 8, 1862, Fremont attacked Ewell’s strong position on the ridge a mile south of Mill Creek. Fremont was repelled and could not take the ridge. Jackson planned to attack the outnumbered V Corps, commanded by James Shields, at Port Republic. Ewell’s division slipped away under the cover of darkness and marched towards Brown’s Gap.

Early on the morning of June 9, Jackson ordered an advance onto the batteries on Coaling Hill. This assault failed, and Jackson ordered the rest of Ewell’s division to cross the North River Bridge and burn it behind them. This would leave Fremont on the other side of the river, alone. Jackson ordered another charge on the Federal batteries, and he was repulsed. Ewell’s men arrived and pushed the Federals off the hill, but they regrouped and repulsed Ewell’s men. After three more assaults were made, the Confederates finally controlled the hill, and repelled a counter attack made by some Ohio regiments. Confederate reinforcements arrived and began bombarding the Federal troops in the flat-lands. The Federal troops then reluctantly began to retreat. Jackson said that it was, “Through God’s blessing,” that the enemy was routed. (Gwyne 327)

Jackson moved to Manassas Junction, captured the Federal supplies, and destroyed them. He then retreated and took up a defensive position, which was effectively inviting General John Pope to assault him. On August 28, 1862, Pope launched repeated assaults at Jackson as Confederate General Longstreet marched towards the battlefield with reinforcements. On August 30, Pope mistakenly thought Jackson was retreating. Longstreet took advantage of this, and slammed into Pope’s left flank. This attack forced the Federals to retreat in a manner similar to that of the First Battle of Manassas, on roughly the same battleground.

On October 10, Jackson was promoted to Lieutenant General. He ranked just below Lee and Longstreet. He was assigned to Second Corps. Before both armies wintered, the Confederate army repulsed a large Federal assault on the right flank of their line at the Battle of Fredericksburg.

Jackson’s last battle was the Battle of Chancellorsville in April 1863. The Army of Northern Virginia faced a serious threat from the Army of the Potomac, led by its new commander, Major General Joseph Hooker. Lee decided to perform a risky offensive on Hooker. He divided his troops and sent Jackson on an aggressive flanking maneuver to the right of the Federal lines. Jackson sent Major General Fitzhugh Lee’s cavalry to do reconnaissance of the Federal line. They found a bunch of relaxed Federals eating, playing cards, and sleeping. Lee describes what happens next:

“So impressed was I with my discovery, that I rode rapidly back to the point on the Plank road where I had left my cavalry, and back down the road Jackson was moving, until I met "Stonewall" himself. "General", said I, "if you will ride with me, halting your column here, out of sight, I will show you the enemy's right, and you will perceive the great advantage of attacking down the Old turnpike instead of the Plank road, the enemy's lines being taken in reverse. Bring only one courier, as you will be in view from the top of the hill." Jackson assented, and I rapidly conducted him to the point of observation. There had been no change in the picture. I only knew Jackson slightly. I watched him closely as he gazed upon Howard's troops. It was then about 2 pm. His eyes burned with a brilliant glow, lighting up a sad face. His expression was one of intense interest, his face was colored slightly with the paint of approaching battle, and radiant at the success of his flank movement. To the remarks made to him while the unconscious line of blue was pointed out, he did not reply once during the five minutes he was on the hill, and yet his lips were moving. From what I have read and heard of Jackson since that day, I know now what he was doing then. Oh! "beware of rashness", General Hooker. Stonewall Jackson is praying in full view and in rear of your right flank! While talking to the Great God of Battles, how could he hear what a poor cavalryman was saying. "Tell General Rodes", said he, suddenly whirling his horse towards the courier, "to move across the Old plank road; halt when he gets to the Old turnpike, and I will join him there." One more look upon the Federal lines, and then he rode rapidly down the hill, his arms flapping to the motion of his horse, over whose head it seemed, good rider as he was, he would certainly go. I expected to be told I had made a valuable personal reconnaissance—saving the lives of many soldiers, and that Jackson was indebted to me to that amount at least. Perhaps I might have been a little chagrined at Jackson's silence, and hence commented inwardly and adversely upon his horsemanship. Alas! I had looked upon him for the last time.” (Lee F.)

Jackson immediately arranged his corps and prepared to charge on the Federal right. The Confederates marched quietly until they were a few hundred yards from the Federal camp, then they released a rebel yell and a full charge. Most of the Union troops were captured or completely routed. Jackson kept pushing towards the Federal center until dusk.

Jackson went out at dusk with some others to do some reconnaissance between the lines. He passed the 18th North Carolina on the way out. Jackson and his party went all the way to the Confederate skirmish line, which was comprised of the 13th North Carolina. He listened to the Federal troops frantically cutting down trees to slow the Confederate advance. When a single shot rang out from a Confederate skirmisher, skirmishers on both sides began to fire at each other. The Confederate main line began to fire and fired into the back of their own skirmishers. As Jackson and his party rode back toward the Confederate line, manned by the 18th North Carolina, they saw what they thought was enemy cavalry closing in at short range. They had no idea that it was their own men. 

The men in the front of Jackson’s group suffered the worst. Jackson was hit by three bullets. One smoothbore round entered above the base of his right thumb, broke two fingers, and buried itself in the back of his hand. The other two bullets were far more destructive. One round hit an inch below his elbow and exited above his wrist. The other round hit him three inches below the shoulder and completely shattered the bone.

His signal officer, Richard Wilbourn, reigned in Jackson’s horse, Little Sorrel, who had taken off toward the Federal lines. General A. P. Hill arrived and the two men ripped through Jackson’s jacket, took off his blood-filled gloves, tied handkerchiefs above and below his arm wounds, and put his arm in a sling. He was placed into a litter and carried toward the Confederate lines. He was dropped twice along the way, both times on his shattered arm, causing extreme pain. Once behind the Confederate lines, he was put in an ambulance that had been brought up, and given some whiskey and morphine. Riding with Jackson in the bed of the wagon was Jackson’s artillery chief Colonel Stapleton Crutchfield, who had been wounded in the leg. Both men asked the driver about the others well being and elevated the others health over their own. Brigade Surgeon Hunter McGuire, after examining Jackson’s arm, decided amputation was necessary. He amputated Jackson’s left arm just below the elbow, and repaired his right hand.

Jackson had good mental clarity the day after his amputation. He sent for his wife to come see him at his recovery room in a private home near Guiney's Station. His men kept fighting in the battle, many of whom cried, “Remember Stonewall Jackson!” or “Revenge Jackson!”. Lee wrote to a friend,“Jackson lost his left arm, but I my right arm.” (Gwynne 545) The Confederate army won the Battle of Chancellorsville and it is considered one of General Lee’s greatest victories.

In the early morning of May 7, 1863, Jackson’s condition suddenly worsened. He developed pain in his side and difficulty breathing. He was diagnosed with pneumonia, brought on by a “contusion of the lung” produced by a fall from the litter. There is some debate among doctors as to whether or not this diagnosis is accurate, but it is generally agreed upon that he had pneumonia. He would have to fight for his life to survive.

Jackson’s wife Anna and his five-and-a-half-month-old daughter, Julia, came to visit him. She stayed with him for the next several days. He was now in a semiconscious state. When he would wake up, he was able to talk coherently to the people in the room before lapsing back into unconsciousness. Sometimes when he was asleep he would talk as if he was in battle: “Tell Major Hawks to send forward provisions to the men,” or “Order A. P. Hill to prepare for action.” (Gwynne 548)
His condition did not improve over the next few days. Eight physicians were called to consult on his condition. He received the best medical care for the time period, which included blood-letting from the chest, applying mustard plasters, and regular doses of laudanum (a mixture of opium and whiskey). He was fading quickly, and he asked Anna and her brother to sing hymns for him. They sang one of his favorite hymns “Harwell”:

“King of glory, reign for ever,
Thine an everlasting crown;
Nothing from thy love shall sever
Those whom thou hast made thine own:
Happy objects of thy grace,
Destined to behold thy face.
Hallelujah! Hallelujah! Hallelujah!”

Jackson was calm and aware of his situation. He said: “I thank God, if it is his will, I am ready to go.”(Gwynne 549)

On Sunday May 10, Jackson’s illness was crushing him. The doctors were not expecting him to live much longer. After lunch his mental strength began failing. At one-thirty he was told that he had a few hours left to live, and he replied, “Very good, it is all right.” (Gwynne 551) At about 3:15 pm he awoke in a delirium, crying, “A. P. Hill to prepare for action! Pass the infantry to the front rapidly! Tell Major Hawks…” (Gwynne 551) Then he was abruptly quiet. Soon a smile came over his face. Then, without pain or struggle, his spirit passed from earth to the God who gave it.

When the news of Jackson’s death reached Richmond, it carried a shock that was increased by its suddenness. Jefferson Davis proclaimed his passing “a great national calamity.” A large group of soldiers gathered outside of the house where Jackson was staying, all with their hats off and many openly weeping. Jackson’s body was conveyed by rail to Richmond where a large crowd, the largest in the history of the city, had gathered to await its arrival. Church bells tolled,  minute guns split the air, and a band played a military dirge. All businesses in the city were closed, and black crape hung everywhere in the city.

At the train depot, Jackson’s coffin was wrapped in a flag, keeping with military tradition. However, this flag was not ordinary. It was the newly issued national flag consisting of the familiar crossed bars of the Army of Northern Virginia, superimposed on a white background. This flag was originally made to fly on the roof of the capital, but Jefferson Davis ordered it to be used to wrap Jackson’s coffin.

Jackson’s body lay in repose in the Governor’s parlor for a few days, and then went on a funeral procession through the streets of Richmond. He was sent by rail to Lexington, his final resting place. His funeral sermon was preached at the Presbyterian church he formerly attended. He was buried next to his and Anna’s first daughter, and close to his first wife Ellie. At long last he was where he wanted to be: in the presence of God, with the just, made perfect in heaven.

Jackson’s legacy as a brilliant tactician cannot be separated from his Christian beliefs. Jackson’s faith, personal discipline, and sense of duty were not only personal virtues, but they were the driving forces behind his success. Jackson’s fearlessness in combat was the result of his fear of God rather than man. His prayer habits set him apart from those around him . His desire to obey God in all things guided all his decisions. In the end, it is his beliefs, not just his battlefield excellence, that define how he is remembered.



















Works Cited

Gwynne, S.C. Rebel Yell. Simon and Schuster, Inc. October 2015

Dabney, R.L. The Life And Campaigns of Lieut.-Gen. Thomas J. Jackson (Stonewall Jackson). 	Richmond, VA., And Philadelphia, PA., National Publishing Company. 1866

Jackson, Mary Anna. Life And Letters Of General Thomas J. Jackson (Stonewall Jackson). Harper 	& Brothers. 1891

Imboden John D., Incidents of the First Bull Run, https://valley.newamericanhistory.org/memory-articles/AM2002
