posts.title: World War I
posts.summary: The First World War was one of the most important events in the twentieth century. It helped shape the world as we know it.
posts.body:
The First World War was one of the most important events in the twentieth century. It helped shape the world as we know it. The great clash of empires, the new technology, the faulty leadership, and the area over which it was fought made the war so impactful. Many people do not understand to a great extent what really happened, and treat it as if it has little relevance to our lives today. Historians have argued about the events in detail for decades, but one thing is agreed upon:  this war was very impactful and important.

The road to war started long before the first battle. The great powers of the world were trying to create larger navies and armies, and better weapons than their opponents. This caused international tensions, and an arms race between Germany and Austria-Hungary, otherwise known as the central powers, and France, Britain, and other countries, known as the allies. The leading generals of both sides were busy creating war plans and practicing their strategies. Many war games were conducted and the plans were constantly being revised or rewritten.

The war was started by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. The group responsible for the assassination was the Serbian Narodna Odbrana (National Defense), along with its secret terrorist wing, ‘The Black Hand’. Their mission was to free all Serbs from their oppressors and create a better Serbia. They were particularly upset by the annexation of Bosnia into the Austria-Hungarian Empire. In early 1914 they saw their chance to change the world.  
			
“A tiny clipping from a newspaper, mailed without comment from a secret band of terrorists in Zagreb, capital of Croatia, to their comrades in Belgrade, was the torch which set the world afire with war in 1914. That bit of paper wrecked old, proud empires. It gave birth to new, free nations. I was one of the members of the terrorist band in Belgrade which received it. The little clipping revealed that the Austrian Archduke Franz Ferdinand would visit Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, on June 28, to direct army manoeuvres in the neighboring mountains. It reached our meeting place, the café called Zlatna Moruna, one night in the latter part of April 1914. At a small table in a very humble café, beneath a flickering gas jet we sat and read it. There was no advice nor admonition sent with it. Only four letters and two numerals were sufficient to make us unanimous, without discussion, as to what we should do about it.”11

-Boijove Jevtic, The Black Hand

Months of planning followed. Some Serbian students were chosen to be the assassins. They were sent to Serbia, trained, and given weapons. Upon their return to Bosnia, they were ready.

On 28 June 1914, the students dispersed into crowds of onlooking spectators that lined the streets of Sarajevo. One of the students panicked during his assassination attempt and failed. A little while later another student hurled a grenade at the Archduke’s open-top car. The grenade missed the Archduke’s car, exploded in the car behind them, and wounded some of its passengers. The other assassins all missed their chances because of the resulting confusion and chaos.  In the confusion, the driver of the archduke’s car took a wrong turn down a side street. He stopped the car, unknowingly, right in front of the assassins. One of the assassins, Gavrillo Pricip, pulled out his revolver and fired point blank at the Archduke. The rounds hit him in the neck and his pregnant wife in the stomach. An account as given by Count Franz von Harrach, describes what the tragic situation was like.
		
“As the car quickly reversed, a thin stream of blood spurted from His Highness's mouth onto my right cheek. As I was pulling out my handkerchief to wipe the blood away from his mouth, the Duchess cried out to him, "For God's sake! What has happened to you?"At that, she slid off the seat and lay on the floor of the car, with her face between his knees. I had no idea that she too was hit and thought she had simply fainted with fright. Then I heard His Imperial Highness say, "Sophie, Sophie, don't die. Stay alive for the children!" At that, I seized the Archduke by the collar of his uniform, to stop his head dropping forward and asked him if he was in great pain. He answered me quite distinctly, "It is nothing!" His face began to twist somewhat but he went on repeating, six or seven times, ever more faintly as he gradually lost consciousness, "It's nothing!" Then came a brief pause followed by a convulsive rattle in his throat, caused by a loss of blood. This ceased on arrival at the governor's residence. The two unconscious bodies were carried into the building where their death was soon established.”2

-Count Franz von Harrach

The members of the Black Hand were quickly arrested and interrogated. They were Bosnian citizens, but it became clear through their confessions that Serbia was behind the assassination. The infuriated Austrians put Serbia’s leaders under intense pressure and it seemed like war was coming.

Austria-Hungarian leaders saw an opportunity to take control of Serbia and strengthen their weakening empire. The foreign minister of Austria-Hungary, Count Leopold von Berchtold, sent his emissary to Berlin asking for the help of Germany in permanently subduing Serbia. Germany was ready for war. The Chief of General Staff, General Helmuth von Moltke, said before the assassination: ”If only things would finally boil over – we are ready; the sooner the better for us.” 

On 23 July, 1914 the Austrians sent a list of ten demands to Serbia and gave them a 2-day time period to respond. Austrian forces were also mobilized and started to march toward Serbia. Serbia had called to Russia for help, and the Tsar, Nicholas II, called for a period of preparation for his troops. The Germans ordered a mobilization of their troops and declared war on Russia on the 1st of August, 1914.

The French ordered a general mobilization on the 2nd of August, but were hesitant to declare war. Their hesitance was because they did not want to upset their ally, Britain. Britain promised France naval support at first, but declared full war on Germany on the 4th of August. The fire had been lit which would set countries ablaze with war. The First World War had officially begun.
After France declared war on Germany, the Germans started to invade France. They were using plans known as the Schlieffen Plan and the XVII plan. The plans were created by the Chief of General Staff, General Alfred von Schlieffen. His basic idea was to knock the French out of the war in one fell swoop before Russia entered the war, and then deal with Russia. However, the Germans would soon find out that the French formed a far more formidable fighting force than they expected.

The new technological advances in weaponry changed the way World War 1 and successive wars were fought. The invention of machine guns, barbed wire, grenades, better rifles, tanks, and artillery greatly increased the efficiency of the weapons. Most of the commanders had to modify their plans to suit the new weaponry.

One of the most important improvements was made in artillery. The Germans were far ahead of the Allies in artillery technology. The German Army employed 150 mm (6 in) and 210 mm (8 in) howitzers in 1914. The typical French and British artillery were only 75 mm (3 in) and 105 mm (4 in). The Germans also used Austrian 305 mm (12 in) and 420 mm (17 in) guns. The British had a 6-inch (152 mm) howitzer but did not like to use it because it was very impractical for many situations. The artillery was the most valuable piece of weaponry to most commanders because they played a crucial role in preparing the ground and the enemies’ trenches for troops to invade.

The war was fought in two major theaters: The Eastern Front and the Western Front. The Western Front was a narrow portion of land stretching from the English Channel to the Mediterranean Sea. It was a long line of trenches, shell holes, wire, and mud throughout the whole war. The Eastern Front was a long area along the border of Russia. The Russians and the Germans were the main combatants on the Eastern front.

Throughout the war, The Eastern Front was not the busiest front, mostly because Russia was further behind other nations industrially. Russia did not have the new weapons that Germany had, but it did have one advantage: Russia had a large population.  However, they had poor diplomacy and little military success throughout the war.

The Russians declared war on Germany and started to invade eastern Prussia on 17 August 1914. The Battle of Stallupönen was the opening battle of the Eastern Front. It was not very successful for Russia. The Germans repulsed their invasion, and they were near where they started. They were successfully driven out of Tannenberg during the Battle of Tannenberg, resulting in the destruction of the Russian Second Army and the suicide of its commanding general. These opening battles were a disaster for the Russians and a precursor to their eventual defeat.

In 1915 Erich von Falkenhayn, Chief of the German General Staff, decided to try and defeat the Russians on the Eastern Front. By mid-1915 the Russians had been expelled from Russian Poland. During the 1915 offensive, the Russian Empire lost the entire line of fortresses along Russia’s western border, thousands of guns, and tens of thousands of people. They had been pushed hundreds of kilometers away from the German and Austro-Hungarian borders. This was largely due to the shortcomings in the Russian command. The one offensive that favored the Russians was the Turkish offensive in the winter of 1915 and 1916. Through much fighting, they eventually captured the Turkish city of Trabzon on April 1916.

In 1916 the Romanians decided to join the war on the side of the Allies. The German high command had to revisit their Eastern Front strategy. They moved some troops to take control of Romania. By January 1917 the Romanian army had been decimated with 200,000 men dead or wounded and 150,000 prisoners of war. The Germans had also taken control of the Poliesti oilfields, which were a significant source of oil west of the Black Sea.
 
By 1917 there was great instability in Russia because of the February Revolutions. The revolutionaries were trying to overthrow the current monarchy and establish something else they deemed acceptable. Women left the factories and marched in the streets demanding the war be ended. Most Russians were in favor of the revolution, but they did not want it to happen during the war. During this revolution the Tsar was overthrown. In October of 1917, Lenin appeared and set up his headquarters at the Smoly Institute. His goal was to get rid of the provisional government that had been set up after the Tsar’s resignation, and set up a “democracy”. In reality, he only made things worse.

By 1918 Lenin’s new government was trying to end Russia’s involvement in the war. A Russian civil war had been raging since November 1917. This did not help the Russians on the Eastern Front. After the signing of the Treaty of Versailles, the war was over for Russia.

The Western Front is the most famous theater of the First World War. It is my personal favorite to study. From the tangled barbed wire, mud, dead bodies, and showering lead from shot and shell to the strategy and technology, the Western Front was the busiest and deadliest place during the war. Thirteen million people died on the Western Front, about five million of whom were civilians.

Trench warfare was the most common method of fighting on the Western Front. Advanced artillery, machine guns, and better carbines made trenches necessary. Trenches were often reinforced with wood or sometimes steel and concrete. Barbed wire was used at the tops of the trenches. Vast, complicated networks of trenches were dug, some of which spanned hundreds of miles. Only by heavy artillery bombardment could an assault be made without massive casualties. The trenches were very well-defended.

After the declaration of war in 1914, the German army began to invade Belgium and France. The German army came within 43 miles of Paris during the First Battle of the Marne, but the British and French were able to force the Germans back. The Germans retreated north and dug in. The Germans and the British then began to try to repeatedly outflank each other to the north. This became known as the Race To The Sea. By the time both armies were satisfied that they could not outflank each other, they dug trenches that spanned from Ypres, Belgium to just north of Switzerland.

The Germans tried to break through at Ypres in the first Battle of Ypres. They were not successful. The battle ended in a stalemate, which made some of the German commanders turn to diplomatic negotiations.

“As a result of the unfortunately widespread catchword ‘the war must be won in the East’ even people in high leading circles inclined to the opinion that it would be possible for the Central powers to actually ‘to force Russia to her knees’ by force of arms and by this success to induce the Western Powers to change their mind. This argument paid no heed either to the true character of the struggle for existence, in the most exact sense of the word, in which our enemies were engaged no less than we, nor to their strength of will. It was a grave mistake to believe that our Western enemies would give way, if and because Russia was beaten. No decision in the East, even though it were as though it were as thorough as was possible to imagine, could spare us from fighting to a conclusion in the West. For this Germany had to be prepared at all costs.” 3

-General Erich von Falkenhayn, General Headquarters, German Army

General Falkenhayn preferred to make peace with one of Germany’s adversaries, preferably Russia, so that Germany could focus more resources on the Western Front. The common thought among his comrades was that they would defeat Russia quickly, so there was no need for negotiations.

The British on the other hand, were more concerned with fighting than negotiation. Britain focused greatly on the logistics and weaponry of war. They worked on improving artillery, rifles, tanks, and ships to try and increase their strength.

Poison gas was used for the first time during World War One. All sides had signed the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907, which prohibited the use of chemical weapons. It was war, so all previous rules soon went out the window. Both the British and Germans tried to use a form of tear gas early on in the war, but it had little effect. Phosphine gas was developed in 1915 and mustard gas was developed in 1917. Both were very deadly, could linger for days, and killed slowly and painfully. During the Second Battle of  Ypres the Germans released a lethal cloud of chlorine gas over the french trenches. It killed most of the front line defenders, and caused those in the rear to flee. The Germans did not have the proper personnel to take advantage of the gap in defenses, so the attack was not as successful as it could have been. The British tried to retaliate at the Battle of Loos, but the wind blew the gas right back into their trenches and caused more British casualties than German casualties. French, German, and British troops all escalated the use of gas throughout the war. 

The Battle of Verdun began in February 1916. The battle took place near the French town of Verdun, which became known as the “fortress” during the war due to its strategic location. The Germans launched an offensive in early February with the objective of breaking through the French lines and quickly overtaking Paris. The French countered this offensive by moving a large number of troops to Verdun. 

The fighting that ensued lasted for over ten months. The battle had massive casualties, with more than 700,000 soldiers wounded or killed. This made it on of the bloodiest battles in history. However, despite the large casualties, the Germans did not accomplish their goal of capturing Paris. 

The French held their position against the German offensive creating a stalemate. This stalemate changed the outcome of the whole war. It delayed the German offensive into France by a few months, allowing for the allies to prepare for their offensive at the Somme and the Hundred Days Offensive.

The Battle of The Somme began in July 1916 and took place mainly around the Somme River. The British headed the attack because of heavy French casualties at Verdun. The battle lasted from July to November 1916.

The French launched their attack on the norther part of the river, while the British launched their attack further south. The main goal was to break through the German lines and capture strategic high ground in the river valley to aid in further advance into Germany.

The tank was also used for the first time on the battlefield. However, they were slow and often got stuck or broke down. The had good potential, but improvements in technology and tactics were needed.  Many lessons were learned at the Somme that helped improve tanks for future wars.

Despite the incredible man power, the Germans held their ground, creating a disaster for the Allies. The British made no real gains from their original position. They lost an estimated 57,000 men in the first day alone. That day would become known as “The Black Day of The Somme.” By the end of the battle, the British had lost around 420,000, the French 200,000, and the Germans around 465,000.

New developments were made in war strategy directly after the Somme. For instance, the British redivided their army to accommodate smaller platoons. At the Somme the smallest maneuverable company was around 120 troops. These were broken down into platoons that consisted of ten to fifteen men.

The battle began with a heavy bombardment on the German lines that lasted about two weeks. The Germans heavily fortified the area and the shelling had no great effect. After the bombardment the British began an infantry assault with around a million troops. The Somme became the largest offensive in World War 1.

The Third Battle of Ypres, also known as Battle of Passchendaele occurred from July to November 1917. This battle was a vivid symbol of the mud, death, and destruction that occurred on the Western Front. General Ludendorff, First Quartermaster-General, German High Command provided a vivid picture of the battle.

Enormous masses of ammunition, such as the human mind had never imagined before the War, were hurled upon the bodies of men who passed a miserable existence scattered about in mud-filled shell-holes. The horror of the shell-hole area of Verdun was surpassed. It was no longer life at all. It was mere unspeakable suffering. And through this world of mud the attackers dragged themselves slowly, but steadily, and in dense masses. Caught in the advanced zone by our hail of fire they often collapsed, and the lonely men in the shell-hole breathed again. Then the mass came on again. Rifle and machine-gun jammed with mud. Man fought against man, and only too often the mass was successful.4

The name "Passchendaele" comes from the small Belgian village that lies between two larger towns, Passendale and Zonnebeke. The battle was largely fought between the Germans and the British, with support from the French and ANZAC Corps (Australians and New Zealanders). The French objective was to gain control of the two ridges south and east of Ypres. The allies would eventually achieve their objective, but not without massive casualties.

The offensive from the Ypres salient was launched on July 31, 1917. The battle began with the French and British pouring about 4.5 million shells, from 3,000 guns, on the German defenses. The purpose of the shelling was to destroy the German machine gunners in concrete pill-boxes and their long networks of barbed wire. However, the constant explosions accompanied by the torrential downpours created a swampy pulverized mire dotted with shell holes full of water deep enough to drown a man. The shells constantly raked the ground, stirring up the remains of soldiers buried in the mud right where they died. The shelling aided in the British tactic of 'Bite and Hold', a tactic in which the British would capture and hold ground. A description from the German perspective shows how terrible the whole ordeal was.

Take a section of the enemy front twenty kilometres wide and three kilometres deep, batter it for fourteen days with a few thousand guns of all calibres, cover it in a few hundred thousands of gas shells, turn everything completely upside down, until nothing could possibly be still moving as far as is humanly possible - then occupy it by way of ten waves [of infantry] supported by machine guns, tanks and planes proceeding in sequence one after the other and protected by a fiery dome. Then advance the artillery through the shell hole area and prevent the enemy from taking any effective counter-action by continuous barrage fire and unceasing individual attacks. After ten days, you take another section twenty kilometres wide and some kilometres deep and repeat the same calculation. And repeat it until you have reached your goal. 5

The British infantry then stormed out into no-mans land dodging shell holes and barbed wire. The British were supported by dozens of tanks and some French troops. The largely untouched German machine gunners mowed down the advancing British troops. The capture of Bixschoote (Bikschote), Pilckem Ridge, and Saint-Julien was a success, for the British from the first wave of fighting.

In the months that followed, thousands of soldiers attacked and counter-attacked in the deep mud that consistently got deeper. John Charteris said in his diary,  “Every brook is swollen and the ground is a quagmire. If it were not that all the records of previous years had given us fair warning, it would seem as if Providence had declared against us.” No significant gains were made for months. By mid-August 70,000 British troops had been killed or wounded. 

On November 6th Canadian infantry advanced a few hundred yards and captured what was left of the village of  Passchendaele. One final assault was made on November 10th to secure the remaining high ground to the east of Ypres. General Haig at last called a halt and the fighting lessened. This gave the British time to rest.

The war at sea during the First World War was unlike that of previous wars. Over all ship technology had greatly improved. The era of wooden warships had gone, and Germany, France, and Britain had started to build dreadnought battleships. Dreadnoughts were large ships driven by steam-powered turbines. They often had at least one big, main gun with several smaller guns and maybe some torpedoes. Aviation was still being developed and was used experimentally. Two-way radio communications, naval mines, and radar were also major developments that changed the war at sea.

Britain had maintained naval dominance throughout most of its history, but Germany began increasing their fleet and threatened Britain's dominance. In 1914, the Allies had 43 large naval vessels, whereas the Central Powers had 20 large naval vessels. Britain and Germany in particular were competing with each other up until 1914 for who could build the most ships.

The main reason for the arms race was to see who could control the English Channel, North Sea, Mediterranean Sea, Black Sea, and the Atlantic Ocean. Most of the naval combat throughout the war was centered in the North Sea. The British Grand Fleet tried to maintain a blockade around Germany to keep supplies from getting in. The naval blockade ultimately starved the German people of food and raw materials.

One of the most famous battles in the naval war was the Battle of Dogger Bank. The British intercepted German radio transmissions that said the German fleet was heading to Dogger Bank. The British decided to intercept the Germans. On a cold January morning, the battle commenced. The British fired upon the German sailors, who were at a brief disadvantage because they could not see through the smoke. The battle raged on for a few hours and the Germans started to retreat. The British pursued and sank several of the German ships. The British sustained some damage to their ships, but overall their losses were light. The Germans, on the other hand, lost some of their best ships and a lot of men. This was clearly a British victory.

The Armistice
By the autumn of 1918, the Germans knew that the war was over. Their citizens were starving, disease-ridden, and starting to revolt. 1.4 million American troops had landed in France and Germany, and the German losses were too great to be able to continue. Those who were fighting alongside Germany started to withdraw from the war, and by November, Germany was fighting by itself.

It was evident that they could not win. The German war officials told the government to stop the fighting. On November 9th Kaiser Wilhelm left his job and resigned. The Germans then asked the US for an armistice, an agreement to stop fighting. The US agreed, and the Germans signed the armistice. The fighting stopped on the eleventh day of the eleventh month at 11:00 am.

Effects
The world would be vastly different without World War One. Around 8.5 million soldiers and 13 million civilians died in the conflict. Many more civilians died due to later effects of the war like toxic chemicals and the influenza that rapidly spread during the war. Whole generations of young men were lost in four years.  

The map of Europe was forever changed. Four dynasties ended during the conflict: the Habsburgs of Austria-Hungary, the Hohenzollerns of Germany, the Sultanate of the Ottoman Empire, and the Romanovs of Russia. France and Britain divided up the nations, and they are largely in the same division today.

Because of this war, many economies were broken, governments overstepped their God-given roles, and a lot of land was destroyed. We must learn from the mistakes that were made, honor those who died for their beliefs, and never let the truth die in our land. If we reject God’s truth, we can expect to have many wars. Give all glory to Christ.

posts.title: An Appalachian Trail Story
posts.summary: A lot of people go missing in the outdoors each year, but not all of them die. A lot of them actually make it out alive. An important thing to take away from this story is to be prepared.
posts.body:
On one cool quiet day the sun shined through the tall green trees at Geraldine Laragay. She had been hiking with her husband and some friends on the Appalachian Trail. They gave her the nickname “inchworm” because she was slower than most of the other people in their group. They had traveled quite a distance on the trail.

She was having a great deal of fun. She loved the outdoors and was frequently hiking or walking on a trail. She was fairly experienced in the outdoors. In the last photo of her, taken near Main,  she had a great big smile stretched across her face. She was a sweet older lady.

However, one day a slight mishap occurred that had great consequences. Laragay had to go to the bathroom and according to the hikers’ manual you had to go off the trail 200 feet so to not disturb other hikers. Before she left the trail she and her husband picked a rendezvous point a little down trail. They both then went separate directions.

It seems that on her way back to the main trail that she got lost. She kept a brief account of what happened to her in her journal. From her journal we can tell that she sent several SOS texts to her husband, all of which were never delivered because of bad cell service.

When she did not show at the meeting place her husband reported her missing. A massive search and rescue operation was launched with both professional and volunteer searchers. After searching for nearly two months there were no results. There were no foot prints, signals, no disturbed terrain, just nothing. The officials said, “People don’t just disappear like that”. The search was eventually called off with no results.

Her remains were finally located 200 feet from the trail by some outdoor enthusiasts two years after she went missing. They found her diseased in her sleeping bag with her journal. According to her journal she survived for 26 days after she went missing, which is incredible for a woman her age. She died from a combination of dehydration and over exposure to the elements.

A lot of people go missing in the outdoors each year, but not all of them die. A lot of them actually make it out alive. An important thing to take away from this story is to be prepared. Geraldine was reasonably prepared. That is partly why she survived for that long. It is also important to know how to navigate in the wilderness. It can prevent you from getting lost in the first place. The one thing Geraldine would want people to do is get outside more and not be discouraged from exploring the outdoors.

posts.title: Democracy Versus A Republic
posts.summary: Which is better, a democracy or a republic?
posts.body:
Two of the most popular forms of government are Democracy and a Republic. Democracy is defined as “government by the people; a form of government in which the supreme power is vested in the people and exercised directly by them or by their elected agents under a free electoral system.”  In a true democracy, each citizen has equal rights and privileges.  A republic is defined as “a state in which the supreme power rests in the body of citizens entitled to vote and is exercised by representatives chosen directly or indirectly by them.” In a republic, certain citizens may have rights and privileges not granted to other citizens.  Both forms have been tried by various civilizations in history. 

In America, we have a republic. However, many people misrepresent our form of government by calling it a democracy.  Ancient Greece had a form of democracy. However, the noble class had more rights and privileges than other classes.  In both cases the forms of government were corrupted by man. 

Due to the depravity of man, we should expect our earthy governments to be corrupted by sin. However, theoretically, a republic is a better form of government than a democracy. Republics align better with Biblical principles such as obeying God’s law and understanding man’s depravity. In a republic, there is a set standard that is followed, whereas in a democracy the people do whatever the majority wants.

posts.title: American Welfare
posts.summary: The American government has believed since the 1930’s that is has the authority to provide for the material well being of its citizens. However, this might not be a good idea.
posts.body:
The American government has believed since the 1930’s that is has the authority to provide for the material well being of its citizens. To do this, they distribute food stamps, fund the Medicaid and Medicare programs, and subsidize Social Security. The justification for welfare is said to be in Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 of the Constitution:

The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States; but all Duties, Imposts and Excises shall be uniform throughout the United States; . . .
The  Franklin D. Roosevelt Administration, 1933-1944, famously began Social Security, as well as the Work Program Administration (WPA). The WPA was started during the Great Depression to give Americans government-sponsored jobs in and effort to boost the economy. This was done because taking a government handout was generally looked down upon at the time. The WPA gave people the illusion that they were supporting themselves and their families rather than taking a handout. In reality they were growing more dependent on the government. Roosevelt signed the 37-page Social Security Act (SSA) in to law in 1935. The SSA offered Unemployment Insurance, Aid to Dependent Children, Old Age Insurance (OAI), and Old Age Assistance (OAA). The OAI gradually developed into the Old Age Survivors and Disability Insurance which is the form of Social Security most Americans are familiar with. 

Since their inception, Social Security and other welfare programs have cost Americans trillions of dollars. We spend a over a trillion dollars a year on people that are on the bottom fifth of the income  ladder. In the fiscal year 2023, the US spent $1.1 trillion on welfare, which amounts to 18% of the federal budget. Most of the money went to low income families, and despite the amount of money spent, it did an extremely poor job of helping people in the targeted communities escape poverty.

If you teach people that they can be provided for if they choose not to work, more people will choose to not work.  There are currently about 7 million people in this country who are unemployed, most of whom are on some form of welfare. The Bible says: “For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat,” 2 Thessalonians 3:9-11. The solution is: “The person who labors, labors for himself, For his hungry mouth drives him on,”Proverbs 16:25-27. If we ignore the way God made the world and pay people to be lazy, we should expect God to judge us.

God did not give the civil government the job of providing support for its citizens. Their job is to wield the sword and punish the evil doer. The reason welfare does not work is because our government is not supposed to do it. God does not reward disobedience. Our nation must stop government welfare.

The church has the responsibility to help the poor and weak. God said: “If there is among you a poor man of your brethren, within any of the gates in your land which the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your poor brother,” Deuteronomy 15:7 and, “for I was hungry and you gave Me food; I was thirsty and you gave Me drink; I was a stranger and you took Me in,” Matthew 25:35.  The church needs to take back its responsibility to help the poor. The church does not have to give out handouts; it must also give proper spiritual aid to people in need. This will actually help them out of poverty, and is something the government can never do.
